The Hadith. A collection of reports documenting the sayings, deeds, and approvals of the Prophet Muhammad, compiled in the centuries after his death. Alongside the Qur'an, it forms the second pillar of Islamic law and theology, known as the Sunna, guiding Muslim life and jurisprudence.

Hadith means report or account in Arabic. Each hadith is a chain of narrators, called an isnad, leading back to someone who witnessed or heard Muhammad's words. Early Muslims orally transmitted hadith for the first 100 to 200 years before major written collections emerged from the ninth century onward.

Six canonical collections are recognized by Sunni Islam: Sahih al-Bukhari, Sahih Muslim, Sunan Abu Dawud, Jami' al-Tirmidhi, Sunan an-Nasai, and Sunan Ibn Majah. Scholars developed rigorous chains of transmission and verification methods to distinguish authentic reports from weak or fabricated ones. This careful scholarship became its own discipline, including biographical dictionaries of narrators and detailed critiques of chain reliability.

Hadith covers ethics, law, ritual, medicine, family life, and spirituality—essentially all aspects of Islamic practice not explicitly detailed in the Qur'an. The Qur'an provides the revealed word of God; hadith provides context and practical interpretation. Different Islamic schools and theological traditions—Sunni and Shia among them—have varying canons and weightings of hadith authenticity.

The Prophet Muhammad's life and teachings are recorded in these hadith collections, which are foundational to Islamic law, called Sharia, to Islamic theology, and to daily religious practice. They remain central to how Muslims understand and apply their faith.
